slides.text: When I took the night-auditor job at the Grand Halcyon Hotel, the manager gave me one peculiar rule: if the vintage brass switchboard ever lit up for Room 412, I was to unplug the cord and ignore it. 'Bad wiring from the 1994 renovation,' he explained. 'There is no Room 412 anymore. We bricked and wallpapered over the doorway thirty years ago after the fire.'

At 3:18 AM during a blizzard that cut off the mountain pass, the lamp above socket 412 blinked red. I pulled the plug, just as instructed, but thirty seconds later the guest in 414 called down furious, complaining that someone next door was pacing in heavy boots and coughing. I took my master keyring and flashlight up to the fourth-floor corridor.

Between 410 and 414 stretched twelve feet of seamless crimson damask wallpaper. No door, no keyhole. Except sitting neatly on the carpet at the base of the blank wall was a silver room-service tray holding two warm porcelain teacups. And pressed into the wet plaster from the other side of the wallpaper was the fresh, steaming outline of a hand.
